title: Building Bridges – AI Custom Chatbots as Mediators between Mathematics and Physics
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-generated learning materials created with a custom chatbot can improve students’ learning experience and performance in the transition between mathematics and physics. The authors focus on a common challenge in physics education: students often struggle to transfer mathematical understanding into physical contexts, especially when working with multiple representations such as graphs, tables, and formulas. The study asks how AI-generated explanations affect emotions, situational interest, cognitive load, self-efficacy, and performance on proportional relationships.

The intervention was a custom GPT built with OpenAI’s GPT-4o and configured to produce age-appropriate, motivating, and factually aligned explanations of proportional relationships across mathematical and physical representations. In a randomized controlled design, the experimental group received a textbook overview plus an AI-generated explanation, while the control group received the same topic overview plus conventional textbook examples. To avoid confounding from digital delivery, both groups used paper-based materials only, and the learning phase lasted 15 minutes. Outcomes included self-report scales for emotions, situational interest, cognitive load, and self-efficacy, followed by a 30-minute performance test on proportional relationships in a physics context.

Participants were 214 sixth-grade students at secondary schools in Germany. The topic had not previously been taught in class. Students were randomly assigned to experimental or control conditions, and the groups were checked for comparability using prior mathematics grade and subject-specific interest in mathematics. The study was conducted in a school-based field setting focused on early secondary learners working at the mathematics–physics interface.

The main findings were that AI-generated explanations significantly increased positive-activating emotions, situational interest, and self-efficacy, while significantly reducing both intrinsic and extrinsic cognitive load. However, the effect on learning performance was mixed and overall inconclusive: there was no significant difference in total test score, though a few individual subtasks favored one group or the other. The authors conclude that custom chatbot-generated explanations can improve the quality of the learning experience, but stronger evidence is still needed to determine whether they reliably improve academic performance or transfer of knowledge over time.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family chatbot product, including custom GPTs built on OpenAI models for tailored instructional support and content generation.
identified_tools.use_case: A custom GPT configured in OpenAI based on GPT-4.0 was used to generate age-appropriate explanations of proportional relationships across graphs, tables, and formulas for sixth-grade mathematics/physics learning materials; students received these AI-generated explanations on paper instead of textbook examples.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized controlled study with N = 214 sixth-grade students, the experimental group receiving AI-generated explanations showed significantly higher positive-activating emotions than the textbook control group (p = 0.00093, d = 0.48). The emotion measure covered pleasure and satisfaction.

No statistically significant group difference was found for negative-deactivating emotions after the learning phase (p = 0.391), although the authors note a trend toward more negative emotions in the control group. The measured emotions were boredom, frustration, and uncertainty.

Situational interest was significantly higher in the AI-generated explanation group than in the textbook group (p = 0.00223, d = 0.45) in the randomized study of N = 214 students. The authors interpret this as a more engaging learning experience.

Students learning with AI-generated explanations reported significantly lower intrinsic cognitive load than students using textbook materials (p = 0.00060, d = 0.47) in the N = 214 RCT. This indicates the AI materials reduced perceived task complexity during learning.

Students in the AI explanation condition reported significantly lower extrinsic cognitive load than controls (p = 0.0001, d = 0.59) in the randomized study with N = 214. This was the largest reported effect among the cognitive/affective outcomes.

Self-efficacy for solving a topic-related task was significantly higher in the experimental group using AI-generated explanations than in the textbook group (p = 0.00001, d = 0.63) in the N = 214 trial. The authors conclude the chatbot explanations fostered students' confidence.

For the overall performance test on proportional relationships in mathematical and physical contexts, no significant difference was found between the AI-generated explanation group and the textbook group (p = 0.750) in the N = 214 randomized study. The authors therefore conclude the overall learning-outcome effect was unclear.
findings.measure: Overall performance test score on proportional relationships / transfer to physics context

findings.finding_summary: At the subtask level, results were mixed: no significant differences were found for subtask A (p = 0.133) or D (p = 0.251), the AI group scored significantly higher on subtask C (p = 0.022, d = 0.32), while the control group scored significantly higher on value 3 (p = 0.016, d = 0.33) and value 5 (p = 0.038, d = 0.29) within subtask B; the overall subtask B score was not significant (p = 0.403). This suggests no clear consistent advantage for AI-generated explanations on immediate achievement.
findings.measure: Performance test subtasks A-D and selected subtask B values; subtask C involved calculating the constant of proportionality

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled study with a relatively large sample (N = 214), which strengthens causal inference. However, it is a short-duration field study using paper-delivered AI-generated materials rather than live chatbot interaction, and the paper notes limitations in generalizability and implementation scope.
impact_tier_rationale: Several reported effects are positive and in the small-to-medium range, including positive emotions (d = 0.48), situational interest (d = 0.45), intrinsic cognitive load (d = 0.47), extrinsic cognitive load (d = 0.59), and self-efficacy (d = 0.63). Academic performance effects were mixed/null overall, but the strongest observed impacts on learner experience exceed the 0.20 threshold.
